title: Temples and Sanghas in Chicago
bigQuestion: What do Buddhist temples in Illinois show about how Buddhists live and practice together?

story.title: A New Temple in a New City
story.kicker: A family leaves a camp in 1944 and helps build a temple in Chicago.
paragraphs: During World War II, the U.S. government forced Japanese Americans on the West Coast to leave their homes. Families were sent to camps behind barbed wire. Many of these families were Buddhist.
In the camps, people still met for Buddhist services. They sat in plain wooden barracks. They chanted and listened to talks. A priest helped them keep their faith and their hope.
Some families were allowed to leave the camps if they moved away from the West Coast. Many came to Chicago. They found jobs and small apartments. But they missed their temple.
In 1944, a Buddhist priest named Gyomay Kubose and a group of Japanese Americans started a temple in Chicago. Today it is called the Buddhist Temple of Chicago. It still welcomes people every week.
story.think: Why might a temple matter so much to families who had lost their homes?

lessons.title: The Buddhist Temple of Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: Japanese Americans founded the Buddhist Temple of Chicago in 1944, after the wartime camps.
reading: The Buddhist Temple of Chicago began in 1944. Japanese Americans leaving the wartime *incarceration* camps started it. Incarceration means being locked up. These families had done nothing wrong.
The temple's first leader was Reverend Gyomay Kubose. He taught in plain English so everyone could understand. He wanted young Japanese Americans and new friends to feel welcome.
Today the temple stands in the Uptown neighborhood of Chicago. It holds Sunday services, classes and festivals. It is part of the long story of Buddhists in *Illinois*.

words.d: being locked up; in World War II, Japanese Americans were forced into camps
our state, home to many Buddhist temples and communities

lessons.title: Services in English
lessons.mainIdea: Many Japanese American temples hold Sunday services with chanting, a talk and music.
reading: Japanese American temples often hold services on Sunday. Many belong to a tradition called Jodo Shinshu, or *Shin Buddhism*. It centers on Amida Buddha.
At a service, people chant together. A minister gives a short talk, called a Dharma talk. Some temples have a Sunday school for children, too. Then people share tea and snacks.
Leaders like Rev. Kubose wanted the teaching in plain words. So many talks are in English. This helps children and new visitors understand the *Dharma*, the Buddha's teaching.

words.d: Jodo Shinshu, a Japanese Buddhist tradition centered on Amida Buddha

look.title: A Sunday Morning

lessons.title: Chicago and 1893
lessons.mainIdea: In 1893, Buddhist teachers spoke in Chicago at the World's Parliament of Religions.
reading: Buddhism came to Chicago's attention long before 1944. In 1893, the city held a great world's fair. Beside it met the *World's Parliament of Religions*.
Leaders of many faiths spoke there. Anagarika Dharmapala came from Sri Lanka. Soyen Shaku, a Zen teacher, came from Japan. They explained Buddhism to large crowds.
Many Americans heard about Buddhist teaching for the first time. Some began to read Buddhist books. Chicago became an early *meeting place* of Buddhists and other Americans.

words.d: a big meeting of faith leaders held in Chicago in 1893
a place where different people come together

lessons.title: Temples from Many Lands
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois has Buddhist temples started by families from many Asian countries and by converts.
reading: Walk around Chicago and its suburbs, and you can find many kinds of Buddhist temples. Some were started by Thai families. Others by Vietnamese, Cambodian, Laotian, Sri Lankan, Korean, Chinese or Tibetan families.

Many of these families came to America after 1965, when the law made it easier to *immigrate*. Refugees from Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos came after wars in the 1970s. They built temples to keep their faith and language.
There are also *converts*. A convert is someone who chose a new religion. Some Americans who grew up in other faiths now meet in Zen or Tibetan Buddhist centers in Illinois.

words.d: to move to a new country to live
people who must leave their country to be safe
people who choose to join a new religion

look.prompt: What do these two temples show about Buddhism in Illinois?

lessons.title: Monks and Nuns
lessons.mainIdea: Monks and nuns give their lives to Buddhist practice, and laypeople support them.
reading: In many temples, you meet monks or nuns. They shave their heads and wear robes. The color can be orange, maroon, gray, brown or black, depending on the tradition.

Monks and nuns study, teach and meditate. In the Theravada tradition, they follow the many rules of the *Vinaya*. The community of monks and nuns is called the *sangha*. Some people use sangha for all Buddhists together.
Laypeople and the sangha help each other. Laypeople give food and needed things. Monks and nuns give teaching and lead ceremonies. Buddhists call this a circle of giving.

words.d: the community of monks and nuns; sometimes all Buddhists together
the part of the Buddhist scriptures with rules for monks and nuns

look.title: Robes of Many Colors
look.text: At an event in Chicago, monks and nuns from many temples stand together. Thai and Sri Lankan monks wear orange. Tibetan monks wear maroon and yellow. Korean nuns wear gray. Japanese Zen priests wear black.
look.prompt: Why might robe colors differ from country to country?

lessons.title: The Alms Round
lessons.mainIdea: In parts of Asia, monks walk each morning to receive food, and families feel glad to give.
reading: In Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Myanmar, many monks walk out early each morning. They walk quietly in a line, carrying *alms bowls*. This is the alms round.
Families wait by the road. They place rice and other food in the bowls. Often they kneel or bow. The monks may chant a short blessing in return. No one hurries.
Monks do not ask for food. They simply walk. Buddhists say the round gives laypeople a chance to practice *generosity* every day. Some temples in America hold a version of this on special days.

words.d: bowls monks carry to receive food as a gift
being glad to give and share

check.q: What do Buddhists say the alms round helps laypeople practice?

lessons.title: What a Visitor Sees
lessons.mainIdea: A temple visitor may see a shrine, offerings, and people bowing or chanting.
reading: When you walk into a Buddhist temple, you often see a *shrine* first. A statue of the Buddha sits in the center. It is placed high, as a sign of respect.
Around it are offerings: flowers, candles, incense and food. You may hear people chanting together. You may see people *bowing* before the statue. Many people sit on the floor.
Buddhists explain bowing in different ways. Many say they bow to show respect for the Buddha and his teaching. They say they are not bowing to the metal or stone itself.

words.d: a place set up to honor a holy person, often with a statue and offerings
bending the body or head to show respect

look.title: Inside the Hall
look.text: The hall is quiet. The Buddha statue sits on a high platform with eyes half closed. Candles glow on each side. A man kneels, puts his hands together and bows three times. Then he sits quietly.
look.prompt: What might the man say his bow means?

check.q: Why is the Buddha statue usually placed high?

check.why: Placing the statue high shows respect.

check.q: What do many Buddhists say they are bowing to?
check.why: Many Buddhists say the bow honors the Buddha and the Dharma, not the material.

check.q: Which might you hear in a temple hall?
check.why: Chanting together is common in Buddhist temples.

lessons.title: Being a Respectful Guest
lessons.mainIdea: Visitors show respect by taking off shoes, speaking softly and following the hosts.
reading: Many temples ask guests to take off their shoes at the door. Floors in prayer halls are kept very clean. You might see rows of shoes by the entrance. Just follow what others do.
Guests speak softly. They do not point their feet at the Buddha statue or at monks. In many Asian cultures, pointing the feet is rude. A guest can sit with feet tucked to the side.
A *guest* does not have to bow or chant. Watching quietly is fine. The best thing a visitor can do is ask the hosts what is welcome. That is *respect*.

words.d: a visitor who is welcomed into someone else's place
showing care for people and what matters to them

lessons.title: One Buddhism, Many Faces
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago's temples show the many ways Buddhists practice, and none is ranked above another.
reading: In one city, you can find Shin, Zen, Thai, Vietnamese and Tibetan temples. Each has its own language, clothing and customs. Some are big, and some are small. Each one is a real place where families meet.
Yet they share some things. All honor the Buddha. All treasure the Dharma, his teaching. All have a sangha, a *community*. Buddhists call these the *Three Jewels*.
Scholars who study religion describe each group on its own terms. They do not say one is the true Buddhism. Learning about many temples helps us see the whole picture.

words.d: the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha, which all Buddhists honor
a group of people who share a practice or a life together

look.title: Two Children Compare
look.text: Ana goes to a Vietnamese temple. Kenji goes to a Shin temple. Ana says, 'We have monks in brown robes.' Kenji says, 'We have a minister and Sunday school.' Both say, 'We honor the Buddha.'
look.prompt: What is the same for Ana and Kenji? What is different?

check.why: Buddhists honor the Buddha, his teaching and the community as the Three Jewels.

check.q: How do scholars describe different Buddhist groups?

check.why: Scholars describe traditions without saying one is the true Buddhism.

check.q: Which do all these temples share?
check.why: Languages and customs differ, but all honor the Buddha.
